amplifyPatterns.pattern: Problem-first routines win when the scalp issue is tied to a specific life moment, not just generic dandruff.
amplifyPatterns.evidence: Amplify videos anchor Head & Shoulders to an urgent or aspirational occasion: oily/flaky scalp from frequent workouts in a summer “Hair Watch Hotline” skit, bridal-era dry/itchy scalp before wedding-related beauty moments, and a quick wash while running late to a watch party. This gives viewers a reason to care immediately and makes the product feel like the practical solution to a real scenario.

amplifyPatterns.pattern: Visible wash/application plus finished-hair payoff separates winners from weaker ads.
amplifyPatterns.evidence: All amplify videos show the product entering the routine: shampoo pumped into hand or shown in shower, lathering/massaging scalp, rinsing or styling, then a finished look. The product role is functional—washing away sweat/oil/build-up, soothing dry itchy scalp, or enabling a fast refresh—rather than just being held as a prop.

amplifyPatterns.pattern: Fast multi-beat structure performs better than a static joke or product mention.
amplifyPatterns.evidence: The amplify videos use frequent cuts and clear progression: hook/story setup → product recommendation or reason → shower/lathering proof → styling or lifestyle payoff → CTA or closing line. Each has 13–18 cuts and keeps visual novelty high across bathrooms, shower shots, styling shots, and lifestyle cutaways.

amplifyPatterns.pattern: Hair reveal must be desirable and connected to the starting problem.
amplifyPatterns.evidence: The winning videos end on glossy blowout movement, soft bridal waves, or clean styled waves after a quick wash. Comments respond with desire and admiration, e.g. “Influenced,” “Brb going to get mine now,” “NEED while I’m in my bridal era,” and “Dude I need my hair to look like that.”

amplifyPatterns.pattern: Distinct branded hooks outperform generic humor: hotline skit, bridal-era secret, and running-late mini-story are immediately understandable.
amplifyPatterns.evidence: Each amplify hook creates a recognizable content package in the first 3 seconds: a retro pink “Hair Watch Hotline,” “My secret for BRIDAL ERA HAIR,” and “running late to the watch party.” These hooks clarify the situation before the product pitch, which likely helped avoid the ad feeling random.

amplifyPatterns.pattern: Comments on winners show purchase intent, not just laughs or passive praise.
amplifyPatterns.evidence: Amplify comment emotion leans toward desire_to_buy/excitement: the hotline video has high purchase intent with comments like “Influenced!” and “Brb going to get mine now”; the watch-party GRWM has comments like “Alright you convinced me, I’m getting them”; the bridal video creates need-state comments like “NEED while I’m in my bridal era.”

stopPatterns.pattern: Avoid static meme-style ads where the product is not visually used or meaningfully connected to the joke.
stopPatterns.evidence: In the stop video from italianbach, the first seconds are a side-profile comedy bit with unrelated dialogue, the shot stays mostly static, and Head & Shoulders Glacier Mint is only mentioned in the caption rather than shown in the sampled frames or applied. This is supported by one stop video only.

stopPatterns.pattern: Do not rely on a long scripted premise if the shampoo proof is only implied.
stopPatterns.evidence: The twin skit has a clear comparison premise and product shots, but shampoo use is discussed rather than shown being applied. The video spends much of its 47 seconds on dialogue and character beats before the final hair reveal, which may have weakened credibility and payoff versus amplify videos that show shower lather and scalp massage. This is supported by one stop video only.

stopPatterns.pattern: Generic humor without a real scalp/hair-care transformation can attract little buying emotion.
stopPatterns.evidence: The stop videos either use an unrelated weird-friend joke or a twin comparison skit with limited product demonstration. Their comments show no meaningful purchase intent; italianbach drew a disappointment/ethical objection comment, while the twin video drew only low-volume praise/trust without desire-to-buy.

stopPatterns.pattern: Ethical backlash can dominate when there is not enough positive product value in the comments.
stopPatterns.evidence: The italianbach stop video’s only cited comment was an animal-testing boycott objection, making disappointment the dominant emotion. This is supported by one stop video only, but it shows that weak creative leaves no positive product conversation to balance brand criticism.

observeNotes.pattern: Sports/team content can beat the brand page through fandom and humor, but often lacks strong purchase intent when the product is mostly a prop.
observeNotes.evidence: Several observe videos use NFL/Detroit Lions or soccer contexts, driving admiration, humor, or excitement. However, product use is usually limited to holding bottles, end cards, locker placement, or captions, so purchase intent stays low except where the itch/flakes problem is made very explicit.

observeNotes.pattern: GRWM routines with real washing steps are closer to the amplify formula, especially when they include a time crunch or occasion.
observeNotes.evidence: Observe GRWMs such as preseason basketball and cheerleader/oral argument include shower use, lathering, blow-drying, and polished reveals. They generated admiration for hair, but comments showed lower purchase intent than amplify videos, suggesting the story or emotional hook needs to be more distinctive or personally urgent.

observeNotes.pattern: Short stat-based product reveals can create awareness but may be too thin for conversion.
observeNotes.evidence: The dandruff statistic video quickly says “one in two people have dandruff” and reveals Classic Clean, but there is no application, transformation, or occasion. Comments skewed humor/disappointment rather than product desire. This is supported by one observe video only.

amplify: Relatable urgency: running late, post-workout scalp, summer sweat, beauty prep before an event
Aspirational identity moments: bridal era, polished confidence, party/watch-party readiness
Visible proof: lather, scalp massage, rinse, blowout, finished-hair reveal
Desire for clean/fresh scalp and hair that still looks styled
Playful storytelling that makes the ad feel like a skit or mini-story instead of a product lecture
Creator credibility through personal problem language: oily, flaky, dry, itchy, build-up
stop: Confusion or irrelevance from humor that does not connect to hair care
Low trust when product use is only claimed, not demonstrated
Viewer disappointment or brand criticism taking over the comment section
Passive admiration without urgency to try or buy
